 Student loan SAVE plan lawsuit: Court allows forced repayment transfers
 Yana Keller 
 Nov 20, 2026 
 5 min 
 Follow Beinsure on 
 Stock Market & Investing News 
 🇺🇸 US Insurance News 
 Why student loan borrowers challenged the SAVE plan repeal 
 Court rejects request to halt forced student loan transfers 
 What happens to borrowers leaving the SAVE repayment plan? 
 Loan servicing problems add uncertainty to the transition 
 What happens next in the Havens student loan lawsuit? 
 Student loan borrowers challenging the Trump administration’s elimination of the Saving on a Valuable Education (SAVE) repayment plan suffered a legal setback on November 18, when a federal court refused to block the Education Department’s mandatory transitions into alternative repayment programs.
 The ruling in the Havens lawsuit denied a request for a preliminary injunction that would have temporarily halted forced transfers while the broader legal challenge continues.
 A federal judge denied a preliminary injunction in the Havens lawsuit on November 18, allowing the Education Department to continue transferring borrowers out of the discontinued SAVE repayment plan.
 Borrowers argued that they should be permitted to enroll temporarily in REPAYE rather than face potentially higher payments under replacement plans. The court found insufficient grounds for emergency relief.
 The underlying lawsuit remains active, but the ruling permits forced repayment transitions to proceed as borrowers face servicing difficulties and uncertainty over monthly payments.
 The plaintiffs argued that borrowers previously enrolled in SAVE should be allowed to enter the Revised Pay As You Earn (REPAYE) plan, which preceded SAVE, rather than being moved into potentially more expensive repayment arrangements.
 The court rejected the request, finding that borrowers lacked standing to pursue certain claims involving potential tax consequences and had not demonstrated the irreparable harm necessary to justify emergency relief based on higher monthly payments or lost interest subsidies.
 The decision does not resolve the underlying lawsuit or determine the ultimate legality of the Education Department’s actions. It allows the department to continue implementing its repayment transitions while litigation proceeds.
 Why student loan borrowers challenged the SAVE plan repeal
 The student loan SAVE plan was introduced during the Biden administration as an income-driven repayment program intended to reduce monthly payments and accelerate debt forgiveness for eligible federal student loan borrowers.
 The program became the subject of litigation in 2024, when Republican-led states challenged its legality. Federal courts subsequently blocked key provisions.
 Congress authorized the plan’s repeal in 2025 through the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act. The Trump administration later accelerated the elimination process through a settlement agreement with the states challenging the program.
 The Education Department has since sought to move millions of borrowers previously enrolled in SAVE into other repayment options.
 Borrowers represented by Public Goods Practice challenged that approach, arguing that the department was required to preserve access to REPAYE benefits during the transition.
 REPAYE was the income-driven repayment framework that preceded SAVE. The plaintiffs contended that its availability would provide an alternative to transferring affected borrowers into repayment arrangements carrying potentially higher monthly obligations.
 The lawsuit also challenged the department’s authority to implement the forced transitions under the procedures it had adopted.
 Court rejects request to halt forced student loan transfers
 The borrowers sought preliminary relief to prevent the Education Department from automatically moving SAVE participants into replacement repayment plans before the case could be fully decided.
 Their request focused on the financial consequences of the transfers, including increased monthly payments and the loss of interest subsidies. The plaintiffs also raised concerns about possible tax-related consequences associated with the department’s actions.
 In its November 18 decision, the federal court concluded that the plaintiffs had not established the legal requirements for a preliminary injunction.
 The judge found that the borrowers lacked standing regarding the alleged tax-related injuries. The court also determined that the evidence presented did not establish irreparable harm arising from increased repayment obligations or the elimination of interest subsidies.
 As a result, the court declined to suspend the Education Department’s transition process. The decision represents a procedural setback for the borrowers rather than a final judgment on all claims in the Havens litigation.
 What happens to borrowers leaving the SAVE repayment plan?
 The Education Department has been directing borrowers enrolled in SAVE to select alternative federal student loan repayment programs.
 Under the transition arrangements, borrowers receive notices from their loan servicers explaining the available options and establishing a 90-day period to choose another plan.
 Those who fail to select a replacement may be automatically assigned to a standard repayment arrangement or a new tiered repayment plan. These alternatives can result in substantially higher monthly payments than borrowers previously faced under SAVE, depending on their loan balances, income and eligibility for other repayment programs.
 The department has also identified the Repayment Assistance Plan, scheduled to become available on July 1, as another option for borrowers seeking an income-based repayment structure.
 The transition has continued amid reported loan servicing difficulties, creating additional uncertainty for borrowers attempting to understand their repayment obligations and available options.
 Loan servicing problems add uncertainty to the transition 
 The forced repayment changes are taking place amid reported administrative difficulties affecting student loan servicers. Some borrowers have experienced uncertainty over transfer deadlines, available repayment options and when their new monthly payments will take effect.
 After the initial 90-day transition period, some borrowers received additional final notices providing another 30 days to select a repayment plan.
 The shifting deadlines have complicated efforts to determine when automatic transfers will occur and what repayment obligations borrowers will face.
 Democratic lawmakers previously urged the Education Department to give affected borrowers more time and clearer information before implementing mandatory transitions.
 In an April letter, lawmakers argued that borrowers needed adequate support to select affordable replacement plans and continue repaying their federal student loans.
 Public Goods Practice, which represents the plaintiffs, raised similar concerns about the consequences of transferring borrowers before the legality of the department’s actions had been resolved.
 What happens next in the Havens student loan lawsuit? 
 The November 18 ruling leaves the broader Havens lawsuit unresolved.
 Judge Loren L. AliKhan of the US District Court for the District of Columbia denied the plaintiffs’ request for a preliminary injunction and administrative stay.
 The court has not yet ruled on the Education Department’s separate motion to dismiss the case. It indicated that a decision on that motion would follow.
 The plaintiffs’ central argument concerns whether the elimination of SAVE legally restored the previous REPAYE repayment framework and whether the department can require borrowers to move into other programs without making REPAYE available. 
 For affected borrowers, the immediate consequence is that the Education Department can continue its existing repayment transition process without the temporary restrictions the plaintiffs requested.
 Borrowers who remain enrolled in SAVE therefore face the prospect of moving into replacement plans that may require higher monthly payments or provide different interest and loan forgiveness benefits.
 The litigation could still produce further rulings affecting the department’s authority and the repayment options available to borrowers. For now, the November 18 decision leaves the mandatory transitions in place while the court considers the remaining legal challenges.
